articles.title: CSSC Offshore & Marine Engineering secures RMB35.8 billion in new orders
articles.summary: CSSC Offshore & Marine Engineering (Group) Company Limited (COMEC) secured RMB35.799 billion in new orders during the first nine months of 2026, exceeding its full-year contract target by a substantial margin. articles.body: CSSC Offshore & Marine Engineering (Group) Company Limited (COMEC) secured RMB35.799 billion in new orders during the first nine months of 2026, exceeding its full-year contract target by a substantial margin. According to a stock exchange disclosure dated 20 October, the Chinese shipbuilder achieved 217.97% of its annual order intake target by the end of September, with contracts covering several containership classes. The company’s 2026 business plan, outlined in its 2025 annual report, had set a full-year contract acquisition target of RMB16.424 billion. The value of orders secured between January and September was therefore more than double the original target. Containership contracts included in order intake COMEC confirmed that its new orders included shipbuilding contracts for containerships with capacities of 1,900 TEU, 3,000 TEU, 5,300 TEU and 6,400 TEU. The disclosure did not specify the number of vessels contracted in each capacity class, identify the shipowners involved or provide individual contract values and delivery schedules. The RMB35.799 billion figure represents the company’s overall order intake during the nine-month reporting period and should not be interpreted as the value of containership contracts alone. The company stated that the orders were secured through its ordinary business operations and had completed the necessary internal approval procedures. Additional approval from its board of directors or shareholders was not required. Expected impact on future performance COMEC expects the execution of its newly secured contracts to have a positive impact on future cash flow and operating performance. The shipbuilder also stated that fulfilling these orders would not materially affect its operational independence or create significant dependence on the customers involved. According to the announcement, containerships are among the company’s principal products, while the counterparties to the contracts have good credit standing and the capacity to meet their contractual obligations. Nevertheless, COMEC cautioned that contract execution remains subject to uncertainties associated with changes in legislation, industry policies, pricing and market conditions. The announcement reflects contracts accumulated during the first three quarters of 2026, rather than shipbuilding agreements concluded exclusively in October.

REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran. The agreements, announced Thursday, cover 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) each from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054. Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. terminals. Pricing will be linked to the Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee. The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March. The attacks damaged two LNG production trains with a combined capacity of 12.8 MTPA, knocking out approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia. While the U.S. contracts will not begin delivering cargoes until the early 2030s, they will give QatarEnergy an additional source of supply outside the Persian Gulf, where energy infrastructure and shipping have faced mounting threats during the conflict. QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio. “This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy. For Cheniere, the agreements secure another major long-term customer for its U.S. Gulf Coast operations. The company currently operates approximately 56 MTPA of LNG production capacity across Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with another 5 MTPA under construction. One million tonnes annually under the new Sabine Pass agreement remains contingent on a final investment decision for the first phase of the terminal’s planned expansion. The deal highlights QatarEnergy’s growing role not only as a major LNG producer but also as an international LNG trader, while adding another long-term source of U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that can reach global markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saipem and Modern Drilling Company have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore new cooperation opportunities in offshore drilling, starting from the Egyptian market and potentially extending to other countries of mutual interest. In addition, the scope of the agreement may include the sharing of expertise and experience, support in project execution, asset management activities, and training services. Saipem emphasizes that this MoU strengthens its position in a strategic market such as Egypt and aims to leverage new industrial synergies to capture growth opportunities in the offshore energy sector. articles.title: SC Ports handles first Isuzu container shipment through Inland Port Greer
articles.summary: South Carolina Ports (SC Ports) has handled the first container carrying production equipment for Isuzu North America Corporation’s new manufacturing facility in South Carolina. The shipment arrived at the Port of Charleston before moving by rail to Inland Port Greer. It marks an early logistics milestone for Isuzu’s...
articles.body: South Carolina Ports (SC Ports) has handled the first container carrying production equipment for Isuzu North America Corporation’s new manufacturing facility in South Carolina. The shipment arrived at the Port of Charleston before moving by rail to Inland Port Greer. It marks an early logistics milestone for Isuzu’s planned production operations in Greenville County. Isuzu selected the location in 2025, partly because of its rail connection to the Port of Charleston. The company expects to begin production at the new facility in 2027. The plant will manufacture N-Series Gas, N-Series Electric and F-Series Diesel trucks. Inland Port Greer supports automotive supply chains Inland Port Greer provides rail connections between the Port of Charleston and industrial customers across the southeastern United States. The facility operates along the Interstate 85 corridor between Atlanta and Charlotte. It offers overnight rail service through Norfolk Southern six days a week, alongside 24-hour gate access. SC Ports completed a $55 million expansion of the inland port in 2025. The project added 9,000 feet of rail infrastructure and increased cargo handling capacity by 50%. Following the expansion, the terminal can accommodate up to 300,000 rail lifts annually. “Having a reliable and efficient supply chain is critical to our long-term success as we establish production operations in South Carolina,” said Yoshi Murakami, Chairman and CEO of Isuzu. SC Ports Director of Vessel Operations & Carrier Sales Tom Boyle, and Chief Commercial Officer Byron Miller recently traveled to Isuzu Global Headquarters in Yokohama, Japan. (Photo/SC Ports) Charleston strengthens automotive logistics connections The first shipment highlights the role of the Charleston–Greer rail connection in supporting automotive manufacturing investments. According to SC Ports, its facilities handle approximately 10% of containerised automotive cargo volumes in the United States, based on PIERS data. The port authority also reported that Inland Port Greer experienced 355% growth during its first decade of operations. SC Ports President and CEO Micah Mallace welcomed the Isuzu shipment and highlighted the inland port’s role in supporting industrial supply chains. The latest delivery represents the arrival of production equipment rather than the start of regular component shipments. Isuzu’s manufacturing operations are scheduled to begin in 2027.

articles.title: Marco Polo Marine expands Korean offshore push with new JV
articles.summary: Singapore-listed offshore vessel owner and shipyard group Marco Polo Marine has established a joint venture in South Korea with local partner NSEL, strengthening its presence in the country’s offshore vessel market. articles.body: Asia Offshore Renewables Marco Polo Marine expands Korean offshore push with new JV Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 0 1 minute read Marco Polo Marine Marco Polo Marine Singapore-listed offshore vessel owner and shipyard group Marco Polo Marine has established a joint venture in South Korea with local partner NSEL, strengthening its presence in the country’s offshore vessel market. The new company, Baramgil Offshore, will focus on vessel operations, management and chartering, with NSEL holding a 51% stake and Baramgil Corporation taking the remaining 49%. Baramgil Corporation is 90% owned by Marco Polo Marine’s Taiwan-based affiliate PKR Offshore, in which the Singapore group holds an indirect 49% interest. The venture has been established with an initial paid-up capital of about $107,000, with Marco Polo Marine funding its investment through internal resources. The company said the move would have no material impact on its earnings or net tangible assets for the financial year ending September 2027. The latest move builds on an existing partnership between PKR Offshore and NSEL, established in 2023 to pursue opportunities in South Korea’s offshore wind sector. The partners made their first move into the Korean market in 2024, deploying a Korean-flagged crew transfer vessel (CTV) for offshore wind work. The MP Corus was among the vessels brought into the market to support wind farm construction activities off the country’s southwest coast. Marco Polo Marine has also been expanding its offshore wind support fleet across Asia. In July, the company secured a multi-year framework agreement with Siemens Gamesa covering two commissioning service operation vessels (CSOVs), primarily for projects in Taiwan, with potential deployments in South Korea and Japan. The agreement is scheduled to begin in 2029, with provisions for an earlier start in 2028. The contract award for front-end engineering and design of the Wisting production vessel’s topsides was handed out to Aibel following a competitive tender involving Norwegian suppliers. This deal covers front-end engineering and further maturation of the design to provide a basis for a decision on project execution, with an option for engineering, procurement, and project management (EPma). articles.title: Rhenus introduces smart picking technology at Merck logistics hub in France
articles.summary: Rhenus has introduced a smart order-picking system at its logistics hub in Strasbourg, France, to improve warehouse operations for science and technology company Merck. Developed with logistics technology specialist Signature One, the solution combines automated weight checks, light-guided picking and digital quality...
articles.body: Rhenus has introduced a smart order-picking system at its logistics hub in Strasbourg, France, to improve warehouse operations for science and technology company Merck. Developed with logistics technology specialist Signature One, the solution combines automated weight checks, light-guided picking and digital quality controls. The Strasbourg facility supports Merck’s operations in Molsheim and processes approximately 2,800 orders daily across three shifts. The new technology aims to improve order accuracy, reduce picking errors and support more efficient warehouse operations. Smart trolleys improve order preparation At the centre of the system are smart picking trolleys equipped with integrated weighing technology. Each trolley can accommodate up to 30 scales, allowing operators to check product quantities and weights during order preparation. Light-guided picking helps warehouse employees identify items more efficiently, while onboard cameras allow teams to review orders when additional checks are needed. The trolleys also feature an ergonomic design and colour-coded identification to help organise warehouse activities. “Our shared objective with Rhenus was to improve customer satisfaction by ensuring that the right quantities are picked for every order,” said Quentin Decoster, Distribution Manager at Merck’s Molsheim site. The technology is particularly relevant to Merck’s operations, where accurate order preparation and product traceability are important requirements. Further warehouse digitalisation planned The deployment marks another step in the 16-year logistics partnership between Rhenus and Merck. In 2025, the companies introduced a logistics shuttle powered by B100 renewable biodiesel between Merck’s Molsheim facility and the Rhenus hub in Strasbourg. The partners now plan to connect the smart trolleys to a wider order-preparation system. Future developments will include integration with conveyor systems, on-demand packaging equipment and other warehouse management tools. The planned improvements aim to connect warehouse processes more closely, from incoming deliveries to final customer shipments.

articles.title: Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey
articles.summary: TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies.
articles.body: Vessels October 22, 2026 · 4 hours ago Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email N5K on back of RV Poseidon with the rig working close to it in the background Credit: Ivan Svrcek/TDI-Brooks U.S.-headquartered geotechnical and offshore survey research and service company TDI-Brooks has wrapped up a critical geotechnical campaign for Cook Inlet LNG, a strategic initiative designed to secure natural gas supplies for Southcentral Alaska, delivering vital subsurface data to support the project's anchor selection and helping bring the developer’s floating import terminal aspirations closer to reality. TDI-Brooks has concluded a geotechnical project for the Cook Inlet LNG project (CI LNG) in Cook Inlet, Alaska, providing its Neptune N5K cone penetration testing (CPT) system for an anchor site characterization study. The work supported the project developer by collecting subsurface soil data to inform anchor selection. According to the U.S. player, the study covered different locations within the project site with a scope of 16 CPTs in water depths ranging from 10 to 25 meters. Operations were conducted from the R/V Poseidon , a third-party vessel working in the region, demonstrating the firm’s ability to deploy specialized geotechnical equipment aboard locally available vessels. The Neptune N5K is part of the company’s range of portable toolkits available for deployment worldwide, which allow clients to pair regional vessel resources with TDI-Brooks’ equipment and technical expertise, providing flexible support for offshore site investigations and infrastructure projects. The Cook Inlet LNG project is an energy security initiative designed to address declining natural gas reserves in the Cook Inlet basin of Southcentral Alaska to stave off a potential energy shortfall for heating and electricity by serving as a near-term bridge solution to import gas. The project is designed to use a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) anchored offshore east of West Foreland, near the existing Osprey production platform, utilizing existing subsea pipelines to minimize environmental and construction footprints. TDI-Brooks’ geotechnical study was done to test the seafloor soil properties to figure out how to safely anchor the FSRU and its infrastructure in Cook Inlet's harsh marine environment. The completion of this study comes months after the U.S. firm was hired by Delfin LNG to provide offshore geophysical and geotechnical survey services for the Delfin deepwater port project offshore Louisiana. articles.title: CMA CGM’s first container train arrives at Hungary’s East-West Gate terminal
articles.summary: CMA CGM’s first container train has arrived at the East-West Gate (EWG) intermodal terminal in Fényeslitke, Hungary, marking a new development in the facility’s growing role in international container logistics. The arrival follows the introduction of Maersk’s container depot and dry port services at the terminal...
articles.body: CMA CGM’s first container train has arrived at the East-West Gate (EWG) intermodal terminal in Fényeslitke, Hungary, marking a new development in the facility’s growing role in international container logistics. The arrival follows the introduction of Maersk’s container depot and dry port services at the terminal earlier in 2026. The presence of both shipping companies reflects growing interest in the terminal’s connections between European rail networks and international maritime transport. Located near the Hungarian–Ukrainian border, East-West Gate connects Ukraine’s broad-gauge railway system with Europe’s standard-gauge network. East-West Gate expands its role in container logistics The terminal was originally developed to support rail freight movements between China and Central and Eastern Europe through Ukraine. However, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 disrupted the planned transport corridor. As a result, EWG Group began exploring new markets and alternative cargo flows. The arrival of CMA CGM’s first container train represents another step in that transition. The terminal is now seeking to serve growing demand from industrial customers in eastern Hungary, particularly in the battery and electromobility sectors. These industries generate significant inbound container volumes. However, lower export volumes create challenges for repositioning empty containers. East-West Gate aims to support more balanced container flows by connecting industrial imports with other cargo opportunities in the region. New opportunities for Ukrainian agricultural exports The terminal is also exploring opportunities linked to Ukrainian agricultural exports. The war has disrupted traditional export routes, increasing interest in alternative transport options for grain and other agricultural products. EWG Group is developing solutions that could allow commodities traditionally moved in bulk to enter containerised supply chains. This approach could create additional opportunities for shipping lines, freight forwarders and agricultural exporters using the terminal. The company also aims to strengthen cooperation with international ocean carriers and other logistics partners. Through these developments, EWG Group is working to establish Fényeslitke as a connection point for maritime container logistics, intermodal transport and conventional rail freight. The announcement did not specify the volume carried by CMA CGM’s first train or confirm a schedule for future services.

articles.title: Nexans, Red Eléctrica to tie Mallorca and Menorca closer with new Balearic power link
articles.summary: Nexans and Red Eléctrica are future-proofing the Balearic Islands' power grid with a strategic new Mallorca-Menorca interconnection.
articles.body: Project & Tenders October 22, 2026 · 4 hours ago Nexans, Red Eléctrica to tie Mallorca and Menorca closer with new Balearic power link Nexans and Red Eléctrica are future-proofing the Balearic Islands' power grid with a strategic new Mallorca-Menorca interconnection. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Nexans French cable systems designer and manufacturer Nexans has been tapped as the preferred supplier for a 132 kV power cable link designed to strengthen the security and resilience of the Balearic Islands’ electricity network and slash Menorca's reliance on fossil fuels. Nexans has been selected as the preferred supplier by Red Eléctrica , Redeia 's subsidiary responsible for electricity transmission and the operation of Spain's power systems, for the Mallorca-Menorca 3 interconnection project, a strategic power infrastructure initiative designed to fortify the security and resilience of electricity supply in the Balearic Islands. The tender launched by Red Eléctrica for this project specifies that the execution of the agreement will initiate a six-month engineering phase for a new 132 kV high-voltage alternating current (HVAC) cable link between Mallorca and Menorca and lay the foundation for a future engineering, procurement, construction, and installation (EPCI) contract. articles.body: The US Department of Transportation has announced a US$2.3 billion investment covering freight and passenger rail projects across 45 states and the District of Columbia. The funding will be distributed through the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Grant Programme. The latest funding round includes 105 projects and is expected to support improvements across more than 2,000 miles of railway track. State, local and private partners will provide an additional US$1.9 billion in non-federal funding. Freight rail and port projects Several projects focus on freight corridors, short-line railways and port connections. Recipient Funding Project Arkansas & Missouri Railroad Company US$33.6 million Track rehabilitation between Fort Smith, Arkansas, and Monett, Missouri Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway US$43.5 million Rehabilitation and modernisation of the Toledo Swing Bridge in Ohio Maine Department of Transportation US$37 million Rehabilitation of approximately 90 miles of railway in northern Maine Aberdeen Carolina & Western Railway US$20 million Track, bridge and crossing upgrades in North Carolina Texas City Terminal Railway Company US$30 million Entrance-gate realignment and rail yard rehabilitation and expansion Wisconsin Department of Transportation US$218 million Track, bridge, crossing and station improvements under the Hiawatha West project The Arkansas and Missouri project will replace rail and sleepers, improve siding infrastructure and install rail lubricators on high-degree curves. In Ohio, the Toledo Swing Bridge project will rehabilitate eight of the bridge’s 11 spans and replace its timber fender systems. The work will enable the bridge to accommodate railcars weighing up to 286,000 pounds. Maine will use its funding to replace rail, sleepers and ballast along approximately 90 miles of track. The project also includes the rehabilitation of a railway bridge deck. The North Carolina project will install approximately 30 miles of continuous welded rail, rehabilitate bridges and modernise level-crossing signals. Port-related freight improvements Texas City Terminal Railway Company will realign the vehicle entrance gate serving the port area and rehabilitate and expand its railway yard. The project aims to address safety conflicts between trains and vehicles entering a petroleum facility. It will also provide additional capacity for petrochemical exports. US Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said the investment would improve short-line railway infrastructure, port connections and rail safety across the country. Federal Railroad Administration Administrator David Fink added that the funding would help short-line railways modernise their daily operations, reduce congestion and improve network performance.

articles.body: Asia Gas Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 159 1 minute read EPS / MMMCZCS EPS / MMMCZCS Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery scheduled for November following sea trials. The newbuilding is the first ammonia dual-fuel commercial vessel to be registered under the Singapore flag and the first of two such ships being built by HD Hyundai for EPS. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and burn it as propulsion fuel, the 230 m long vessel is fitted with Everllence’s 6G60ME-LGIA two-stroke engine, which completed factory acceptance testing in April and passed type approval testing in June. The ship features four cargo tanks and dedicated ammonia fuel handling and safety systems, including leak detection and emissions management equipment. The project dates back to June 2022, when EPS joined forces with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and classification society ABS to develop an ammonia-powered gas carrier. The partners have since worked on the vessel’s design, safety requirements and regulatory approval, with particular attention to ammonia handling, ventilation, emissions and crew preparedness. The milestone also coincided with EPS signing a strategic partnership with the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping during the naming ceremony. The two will collaborate on alternative fuels, dual-fuel propulsion, energy efficiency and ammonia safety, including research into methane and ammonia emissions. A joint white paper covering VLAC design, operational safety and crew training is expected later this year. The development adds to EPS’s expanding position in the ammonia carrier market. Earlier this year, the company returned to China’s Jiangnan Shipyard for two additional 90,000 cu m VLACs, scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2028. Those vessels will feature LPG dual-fuel propulsion, rather than engines designed to burn ammonia. The latest contract followed a series of six 93,000 cu m VLACs previously booked at Jiangnan, as EPS continued building up its gas carrier fleet alongside investments in alternative propulsion technologies. articles.summary: Regulatory uncertainty and limited shipbuilding capacity could delay the wider adoption of alternative marine fuels beyond 2030, shipping executives said, while orders for methanol-capable vessels may not translate directly into demand for the fuel. articles.body: Shipowners warn fuel transition could slip beyond 2030 as methanol demand remains uncertain in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Regulatory uncertainty and limited shipbuilding capacity could delay the wider adoption of alternative marine fuels beyond 2030, shipping executives said, while orders for methanol-capable vessels may not translate directly into demand for the fuel. Speaking at the tenth Annual International Shipping Forum in Pudong, Shanghai, Safe Bulkers president Loukas Barmparis said ambiguity over decarbonization rules and heavily booked shipyards would delay the transition, pointing to a period after 2030 toward 2035. He described maritime decarbonization as “somehow stalled,” with progress currently concentrated on improving the energy efficiency of existing ships and newer vessel designs. Uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s decisions had held back ordering before prompting owners to choose conventional vessels, said Dario Bocchetti, Grimaldi Group’s head of energy-saving, research and design, and ship design. Similarly, Pacific Carriers Limited CEO and managing director Hor Weng Yew said owners could focus on improving fuel efficiency while weighing longer-term fuel decisions. “Making an irreversible commitment when the fuel pathways, infrastructure, and economics are still evolving… I think that’s tough,” Hor said. However, owners could retrofit ships and work with charterers to improve efficiency without waiting for a final fuel pathway, he said. “That’s something shipowners can very well do, very much in their control.” Orders may not translate to demand Meanwhile, dual-fuel vessels, such as new methanol-capable orders, may not ensure that a new ship will operate entirely on methanol, Bocchetti added. Fuel costs and logistics would determine actual use, while producers need demand from more than a handful of owners to support supply growth. “Nevertheless, we have to start it; otherwise, we will never do it,” he said. DNV said more than 294 methanol-capable vessels were on order globally as of August 2026, making methanol the second-largest alternative-fuel technology in the orderbook after LNG, based on its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050, released in August. The figure stood at 991 for LNG-capable vessels, 42 ammonia-capable, and 25 hydrogen-capable vessels. The forecast puts shipping’s low-greenhouse-gas fuel demand, covering low-GHG fuels collectively, at 4 million–22 million mt of oil equivalent in 2030, depending on regulatory outcomes. DNV noted that scaling production depends on confidence that demand will materialize. It also said the existing fleet and orderbook would largely determine which fuels shipping can consume in 2030. Marine Plus president and CEO Dimitris Vranopoulos said fuel supply and trading patterns would continue to constrain owners’ investment in dual-fuel vessels. “Even post-2030, it will be quite difficult and challenging,” Vranopoulos said, adding that “everything has to be synchronized.” Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed Singapore low-carbon methanol at $1,040/mt Oct. 19, unchanged from the prior session, while low-carbon methanol FOB Shanghai was also assessed stable day over day at $815/mt on thin trade. articles.title: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel
articles.summary: Global average crude freight rates have climbed above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago, according to Goldman Sachs analysis released Wednesday. The increase initially started in the very large crude carrier segment and on Middle Eastern routes before spreading to all major crude trading routes,...
articles.body: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Global average crude freight rates have climbed above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago, according to Goldman Sachs analysis released Wednesday. The increase initially started in the very large crude carrier segment and on Middle Eastern routes before spreading to all major crude trading routes, particularly affecting long-haul voyages. The bank identified five main drivers behind the $20 per barrel year-over-year surge in the average global crude freight rate. A war risk premium in Hormuz accounts for $7 per barrel, representing one-third of the increase in the global average crude freight rate. Ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf that tie up tankers for longer add $4 per barrel, while higher maritime fuel prices contribute another $4 per barrel. Inefficient tanker allocation and increased tanker redirections account for $3 per barrel, and the blockage of the Iranian fleet adds $2 per barrel by boosting demand for non-sanctioned crude tankers. While global freight rates have declined slightly in recent days, likely due to an easing in the risk premium, the global average remains seven times higher than a year ago. Goldman Sachs expects these factors to continue supporting global freight rates as long as the conflict in the Middle East persists. The bank noted that high freight rates may reduce refiners’ overall demand for crude or shift it towards more closely located crude suppliers. Most traded crude benchmarks do not directly include transportation costs in their prices, as they are priced on a free-on-board basis. Goldman Sachs sees high freight rates widening crude price differentials by changing crude trading patterns and supporting refined product prices while suppressing refiners’ net margins. Crude producers with greater dependence on distant buyers may need to discount their crude more heavily to retain demand from refiners facing high transportation costs. Refiners with greater dependence on imported crude from distant suppliers would need to either pass higher freight costs on to final consumers or accept lower net refinery margins. articles.title: The Unbroken Glass: Bab al-Mandab and the risk of asymmetric escalation
articles.summary: Alliances are drafted for contingencies their signatories hope will remain theoretical. The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement – concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan – was one such instrument, yet early this week, less than two months after it was signed, the three states announced the activation of...
articles.body: The Unbroken Glass: Bab al-Mandab and the risk of asymmetric escalation in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Alliances are drafted for contingencies their signatories hope will remain theoretical. The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement – concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan – was one such instrument, yet early this week, less than two months after it was signed, the three states announced the activation of its collective deterrence measures. What set it in motion was not an invasion, nor the act of a rival state, but a campaign by a non-state movement based in the northern highlands of Yemen. It may prove the first of many state responses in this particular area. The risk differs from that which markets have watched at Hormuz, a problem of leverage in which any actor able to threaten a narrow gateway can impose costs far beyond its physical power. Bab al-Mandab is where the workaround runs. Saudi loadings at Yanbu, on the Red Sea, rose more than sixfold in March, from roughly 0.8 million barrels per day to about 5 million bpd, once Hormuz was effectively shut. Around 80% of that volume initially moved south through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, until that route was jeopardized by the Houthi campaign launched in July. This presents a different vulnerability – asymmetric escalation – where a limited action by an actor of modest means and loose control draws disproportionate responses from many more powerful ones, none of which intends to engage in a wider war. The asymmetry has three dimensions: of scale, since a narrow act produces broad consequences; of actor, since a movement acts while states and alliances must respond; and of control, since no one involved can ultimately determine where the sequence ends with certainty. The same maritime system has produced this pattern before. In 1956 the crisis at Suez owed little to the quarrel over the canal that started it. Britain, France and Israel each came to the same waterway by a different road, the superpowers were drawn in behind them, and an Egyptian dispute ended as a verdict on the limits of post-war European power. Suez is the best template for what follows, with one difference: the party that began that quarrel was a state that could be negotiated with and pressured. The Houthis are not that. The sequence Houthi missile salvos fired at Israel in March widened over the summer into a campaign that broke the militia’s four-year ceasefire with Saudi Arabia. On 20 July the Houthis declared an embargo on Saudi vessels while indicating that other shipping could pass. Most vessels, reportedly, still pass Bab al-Mandab without incident, but weekly transits through the strait fell from 354 – the highest total since December 2023 – to 269 in the first week of the embargo. In September the campaign changed in kind. Drone strikes on 10 September, which Riyadh attributed to launches from Iraqi territory, damaged pumping stations on the East-West pipeline, the kingdom’s principal export artery since Hormuz was constrained. The line restarted on 22 September at reduced rates. In mid-September the Houthis also reportedly took control of the port of Mocha and Perim Island. Yemeni government forces say they retook Mocha on 5 October, but this is refuted by the Houthis. This is no longer only a maritime problem; it is a national security question for the state targeted. The shoreline is of vital strategic importance. Perim divides the strait’s narrowest point into two lanes, the Large Strait of about 17 kilometers and the Small Strait of 2.5 to 5 kilometers. A position on the island would let the Houthis rely on cheap, replenishable weapons, such as sea mines and explosive drone boats, and could allow them to impose transit fees, as Iran has attempted at Hormuz. So far, the pressure has been selective. That is the asymmetry of scale: inexpensive means, expensive consequences. The actor matters as much as the geography. Iran has helped develop the Houthis’ capabilities, but sponsorship is not traditional command and control. Tehran can enable and influence Houthi action without determining every decision. A sovereign government weighs its territory, economy and diplomatic relationships before it uses force; a non-state movement carries a different ledger. Even if the blockade is a bargaining move rather than a bid for wider war, a bargaining move by one party can become the trigger for another. This is the asymmetry of actor: in 1956 Washington’s financial pressure on the British pound halted the Anglo-French operation against Egypt within days, but no comparable lever exists over a movement in the Yemeni highlands. Why responses compound The Makkah agreement shows the sequence is in motion, at least politically. It went unused for two months while Pakistan and Turkey, which had positioned themselves as mediators in the wider conflict with Iran, weighed their roles. The commitment made on 5 October was an announcement pertaining to collective deterrence measures, not a deployment. No troop numbers or dates have been given, Pakistan’s forces were already in Saudi Arabia in supporting roles, and Turkey’s parliament has yet to ratify the pact, although statements from Islamabad and Ankara on 8 October may define the commitment and accelerate it. Amid such escalation, each response may be proportionate: a defensive deployment is read as preparation for offense, a naval escort as a widening commitment, a commercial diversion as evidence that disruption is permanent. Suez is again the guide. Each of the 1956 participants acted on what looked like a sound reading of its own interests, and the sum was a canal blocked by sunken ships, a disrupted European oil supply and a British prime minister who resigned within months. No one chose the whole. That is the asymmetry of control: each decision is reasonable on its own terms, and their sum is not. The same asymmetry also supplies reasons for restraint. A cheap provocation is expensive to answer, and the stronger parties know it. Saudi Arabia has little appetite for another prolonged confrontation with the Houthis, and Turkey and Pakistan have even less reason to be drawn into direct combat, which is consistent with the supporting roles they have so far described. Suez points the same way: the escalation was bounded within days, and Britain’s prime minister paid with his office for pushing it. Where the cost lands Each workaround has become the next chokepoint. When Hormuz was effectively shut after the war began on 28 February, Middle East crude loadings fell from about 19.4 million barrels per day in February to about 10 million in March, and the Red Sea became the main outlet for Saudi crude. As the Houthi campaign pushed vessels north, away from the southern route, Egypt’s Sumed pipeline, with 2.5 million bpd of capacity, absorbed much of the diversion. Crude is offloaded at the Red Sea end, piped across Egypt and reloaded on the Mediterranean coast. The Suez Canal cannot do that job on its own, because only vessels up to Suezmax size can transit it fully laden, so the largest crude carriers loading on the Red Sea either depend on Sumed or must still pass south through Bab al-Mandab. A barrel rerouted away from one chokepoint inherits the risk of another. The adaptation is not temporary, and Suez set the precedent. When Egypt closed the canal in 1967 it stayed shut until 1975, and shipowners responded by building ever larger tankers that made the long route around the Cape of Good Hope economic. Sumed itself was completed in 1977 as a consequence. The detour became the standard route, and the ships built for it could no longer use the canal fully laden even after it reopened. Vessel tracking shows the same pattern in LNG today. In 2023, about a third of US LNG exports to Asia went through Suez. After mid-January 2024, the trade virtually stopped using the canal, and by 2025 a dominant 88% went via the Cape. The cost of the cascade shows in prices. Brent traded above $108 in mid-September and hovered between $98 and $101 in the first week of October. July price scenarios spanned from roughly $65 under full resolution to about $148 if fighting escalated and Bab al-Mandab were disrupted; some of this is being borne out now. Freight has changed too, as shipowner earnings on a direct Saudi-to-China VLCC voyage passed $1 million a day in September, and the shuttle arrangements then in use lifted the cost of landing a barrel in China to about $26, from around $2 before the conflict. Resilience, in other words, is relative: a bypass that funnels through its own chokepoint is less protective than it looks on a map, so the useful question is how many actors a route depends on. That favors diversified supply and shorter, less contested routes to market. Gulf producers remain indispensable. Atlantic Margin basins are a complement, not a replacement, with constraints of their own but less exposure to a non-state actor able to set off a cascade that no one fully controls. Containment Three conclusions follow. The actor is of limited means and loosely controlled, so deterrence works imperfectly. Responses are individually proportionate and collectively not, so every defensive step alters the calculations of others. And markets can absorb a longer route but have yet to price a cascade. The central case remains a shock without a reset, as rerouting, spare pipeline capacity and longer voyages have so far absorbed the strain. Duration, however, is the variable. The longer the crisis persists, the greater the chance that a shock becomes a reset, as Suez did. Whether the cascade is widening will show first in the energy flows rather than in the communiqués – in Yanbu loadings recovering toward their pre-attack level, in Sumed throughput, and in southbound transits by VLCCs. The Makkah agreement was drafted for a contingency the alliance hoped would not materialize. It has now been invoked; how far it is tested is yet to be seen. Suez ended as a verdict on the limits of power, and Bab al-Mandab may yet deliver another verdict on the limits of control. The glass has not broken, and fatigue, cost and the example of Suez all work to keep it intact. But it has cracked in plain view, and the pressure is spreading through every connection the region has. If it does shatter, it may well be on the rocks of the aptly named Gate of Lamentation. articles.body: MMI Daily Iron Ore Index Report October 22 2026 in Chinese iron ore and steelmaking prices 22/10/2026 Today’s decline extended across domestic futures, port spot and seaborne markets, testing the earlier recovery again. DCE most-traded closed at 669.0 yuan/mt, down 1.83%, and all eight Qingdao products fell 9 yuan/wmt. The seaborne 61% index eased to USD 88.60/dmt and the 65% to 106.25, with all 12 brands lower. The aligned price moves indicate that isolated improvements in offers have not generated durable upward momentum. Production has nevertheless improved at the margin. Surveyed daily hot metal output was 2.3584 million mt on Oct 21, up 6,400 mt from the previous period, alongside a modest increase in the blast furnace operating rate. Higher output is not the same as discretionary restocking: mill stocks, end-user orders and margins still shape purchasing schedules. Lower arrival flows may ease future supply pressure, but existing inventory still requires transactions and collections for absorption. The near-term question is whether lower prices generate persistent demand. articles.title: Panama Canal Reports Growth in Transits and Tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026
articles.summary: The Panama Canal recorded growth in both vessel transits and tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026. articles.body: Panama Canal Reports Growth in Transits and Tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026 in Port News 22/10/2026 The Panama Canal recorded growth in both vessel transits and tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026. The results underscore the waterway’s ability to meet the demand of global maritime trade while continuing to adapt to the effects of El Niño. The Panama Canal presented its FY2026 results today during a call hosted by Anna Milne, Managing Director of Emerging Markets Corporate Research at Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta, Deputy Administrator Miguel Lorenzo, and Vice President of Finance Juan Mojica discussed the canal’s water management strategy and progress on initiatives under its Vision 2025–2035, including the Río Indio Lake Project. Operational Performance The Panama Canal handled 13,951 transits in FY2026, up 4.1% from 13,404 in FY2025. Growth was driven by energy shipping segments and strong containership performance. Tonnage reached 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, an increase of 6.5% from 489.2 million PC/UMS tons the previous fiscal year. Vessels transiting the Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with tonnage through these locks rising 8.2% year over year. This growth reflects the increasing share of larger-capacity vessels using the waterway. The results reflect a sustained recovery in demand, supported in part by shifts in international trade flows. The Panama Canal also maintained a maximum draft of 50 feet throughout the dry season, providing favorable operating conditions for its customers. Total revenue for FY2026 reached B/. 6.6 billion, an increase of 16.6% over the previous fiscal year. These unaudited figures reflect strong financial discipline and will support investment in strategic projects that will shape the future of the canal. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Administrator Espino de Marotta said during the call. Results from FY2026 also highlight the performance and dedication of the canal’s workforce and its ability to deliver strong results in a complex global environment. Last Minute Reservations With water conservation measures proving effective and recent rainfall in the watershed approaching average levels, the Panama Canal announced today, through an Advisory to Shipping, the immediate reinstatement of its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service gives vessels without a reservation an additional opportunity to secure a transit slot when one becomes available and the canal, at its discretion, chooses to offer it. The Panama Canal remains committed to closely monitoring water conditions and rainfall and will promptly communicate any further adjustments as circumstances require. The partnership will bring mas’s widebody freighter capacity onto the Freightos platform. Freight forwarders will be able to book cargo space in real time and complete payments through an integrated digital system. It will provide access to mas’s dedicated freighter network serving destinations throughout Latin America. Once the integration is available, freight forwarders will be able to search for capacity, make bookings and arrange payments through the same platform. The service aims to reduce manual booking procedures and simplify payment arrangements. Flexible payment options are also expected to help forwarders manage cash flow when securing cargo space. “By pairing mas’s dedicated widebody network with Freightos Pay, we are replacing administrative friction with instant execution,” said Pablo Pinillos, CEO of Freightos. Expanding access to Latin American cargo capacity The partnership will give mas another digital distribution channel for its freighter services. It will also provide freight forwarders with additional options for booking main-deck cargo capacity on routes connecting North America and Latin America. According to Eduardo Cedilli, Senior Manager, Sales at mas, the integration will help the airline reach more freight forwarders while simplifying its booking and payment processes. The companies expect the partnership to support faster bookings and improve access to available capacity. However, Freightos has not announced a launch date for the integration or specified how many aircraft will be included.

Join the leading maritime news network By David Brunnstrom WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) – The Philippines is exploring deeper cooperation with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables and addressing “gray-zone” activity, despite Manila’s one-China policy, which recognizes Beijing and not Taipei, a Philippine diplomat said on Wednesday. The Philippines and Taiwan have repeatedly complained about Chinese activities designed to pressure the countries without direct confrontation. China claims Taiwan as its own territory and has overlapping claims with both Taiwan and the Philippines in the South China Sea. Felipe F. Carino III, Manila’s deputy chief of mission in Washington, told a seminar this “pragmatic and practical approach” with Taiwan was necessary to protect mutual interests in the Bashi Channel between Taiwan and the Philippines. Speaking to Washington’s Center for a New American Security, Carino linked cable security to South China Sea tensions, but did not mention China by name. He said security of undersea cables was vital given that they carried nearly all intercontinental data flows “and that 60-67% of cyber incidents happen in our region.” “These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan,” Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so “notwithstanding our one China policy.” He said the Philippines and Taiwan were exploring “practical and more pragmatic approaches in cooperation, including knowledge-sharing and capacity building” and added: “We see this cooperation leading towards … addressing the gray-zone issues in our part of the world.” China warned the Philippines that it should “strictly adhere to the one-China Principle with real actions” and sent Taiwan a similar message, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday. Asked if this cooperation could include joint patrols or accountability for vessels that disrupt communications, Carino said he did not have details, but said: “I’m sure that this is a constantly evolving cooperation, and some of the things that you mentioned may be actually coming to fruition.” Taipei has stepped up efforts to protect undersea communications links, which are vital to the island’s connections to the rest of the world, after several incidents involving cables and China-linked vessels. This month, the Philippines’ coast guard said it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge a Chinese research ship operating off northern Batanes province near undersea cable corridors . At the same seminar, Andrea Yang, Taiwan’s deputy representative in Washington, referred to the jailing in Taiwan of a Chinese ship captain over damage to an undersea cable. She said Taiwan would put more resources into developing unmanned systems to improve maritime surveillance. Yang said interference with undersea cables was an issue that should be taken up by the United Nations, which should consider mechanisms to prevent “bad behavior.” (Reporting by David Brunnstrom; Additional reporting by Eduardo Baptista in Beijing; Editing by Don Durfee, David Gregorio and Xevi Fontdegloria) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. Brent crude climbed above $112 a barrel on Thursday as the violence heightened concerns about further disruptions to Saudi supplies. “Commercial storage available through partners is limited. The larger capacity lies in what we call strategic storage owned by governments,” Nasser said in an interview with Al Arabiya on Thursday. “The Ministry of Energy is working with its counterparts in other countries to make strategic storage available for Aramco.” The company already holds commercial oil storage in South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and Egypt’s Mediterranean export hub of Sidi Kerir. “We have maintained these overseas inventories for many years, but we are working to expand them, particularly in Asia,” Nasser said. Aramco wants to double its overseas capacity, Nasser said, without giving a timetable for the expansion or disclosing current capacity. The push forms part of a broader effort to reinforce Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure and export options during the regional crisis. Aramco currently has three main export corridors — the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean. The conflict prompted the company to begin engineering studies to increase its capacity to move crude from the Persian Gulf in the east to the Red Sea in the west to 10 million barrels a day from 7 million, alongside work on other routes, Nasser said. “We did not wait for the crisis to end,” Nasser said. articles.title: OneSubsea and oil & gas giants are unlocking deeper waters with all-electric subsea tech
articles.summary: Out with hydraulics, in with electric: OneSubsea, TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron have tested all-electric tech at depths up to 3,000 meters.
articles.body: Technology & Innovation October 22, 2026 · 8 hours ago OneSubsea and oil & gas giants are unlocking deeper waters with all-electric subsea tech Out with hydraulics, in with electric: OneSubsea, TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron have tested all-electric tech at depths up to 3,000 meters. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Brazilian waters served as testing ground for all-electric subsea technology project targeting deepwater fields down to 3,000 meters Source: OneSubsea Pushing deeper into offshore frontiers, OneSubsea, a joint venture backed by SLB, Aker Solutions and Subsea7, has cleared a critical path for deepwater development through a joint industry project with France’s TotalEnergies, Norway’s Equinor, the UK’s BP, and the U.S.-headquartered Chevron to master all-electric subsea technology designed to operate 3,000 meters below the surface. OneSubsea has completed the Brazil All-Electric Joint Industry Project (JIP) , a collaboration with TotalEnergies, Equinor, BP, and Chevron, supported through the National Petroleum Agency (ANP) research and development regulation, to advance fully electric subsea production technologies for applications at water depths of up to 3,000 meters. The subsea player emphasizes that electrification can create new options for designing and operating future deepwater fields by replacing hydraulic actuation with electric systems and connecting subsea equipment, well completion technology, topside controls, and digital capabilities. The Brazilian project qualified electric components and control systems for deepwater applications and demonstrated an integrated architecture extending electrification beyond the subsea tree, connecting subsea production equipment with electric well completion technology, topside controls, and digital capabilities. Representatives from the participating companies recently gathered at the OneSubsea manufacturing facility in São José dos Pinhais, Brazil, to celebrate the completion of the project through technical presentations, demonstrations of subsea and downhole all-electric technologies, and a tour of the facility where electrified subsea equipment will be assembled. Darcy Ryan , Product Manager at OneSubsea, commented: “Completing this project is an important step toward expanding the role of fully electric technology in future deepwater developments. By working closely with operators to define requirements and qualify the technology, we are creating new possibilities to simplify subsea infrastructure while providing greater control, monitoring and access to data.” As subsea developments move into deeper water and increasingly complex environments, OneSubsea points out that operators are looking for new ways to simplify infrastructure, improve control, and create greater flexibility in how future fields are designed. Since traditional hydraulic systems require extensive distribution infrastructure to operate subsea equipment, adding complexity as developments extend farther from existing facilities, the company believes that this is where all-electric can make a difference. “Conventional subsea production systems use hydraulic pressure to actuate valves and chokes, requiring hydraulic distribution infrastructure across the field. All-electric technology replaces hydraulic actuation with electric motors, eliminating the need for hydraulic fluids and reducing associated infrastructure,” elaborated OneSubsea. The firm explains that the Brazilian project demonstrates how electrification can move beyond individual components toward an integrated production architecture that connects subsea equipment, well completion technology, topside controls, and digital systems. Aside from qualifying components for applications at depths of up to 3,000 meters, the project pinpointed interfaces with newly developed and qualified SLB electric completion technologies. OneSubsea underlined: “A purpose-built master control station connects the subsea equipment with topside control and digital systems, enabling an integrated approach to monitoring and operating the production system. “This architecture can simplify field layouts and reduce overall system complexity while giving operators greater flexibility when developing longer tiebacks, more remote fields, and increasingly autonomous operations.” The company states that the completion of the project builds on more than 15 years of experience in subsea electrification and more than 5 million operating hours with electrified subsea systems. The firm’s all-electric portfolio is advancing along two complementary paths, with all-electric subsea production technology moving toward commercial deployment through Equinor’s Fram Sør project in Norway, which includes 12 all-electric subsea trees . articles.title: Global shipbuilding boom moves into overdrive
articles.summary: The global shipbuilding boom is gathering pace, with orderbooks surpassing their previous 2008 peak, Chinese yards tightening their grip on the market and tanker owners increasingly turning to inexperienced builders to secure delivery slots. New figures from BIMCO put the global orderbook at 203.2m compensated gross...
articles.body: Shipyards Global shipbuilding boom moves into overdrive Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 1 2,289 1 minute read Hengli Hengli The global shipbuilding boom is gathering pace, with orderbooks surpassing their previous 2008 peak, Chinese yards tightening their grip on the market and tanker owners increasingly turning to inexperienced builders to secure delivery slots. New figures from BIMCO put the global orderbook at 203.2m compensated gross tonnes (cgt) at the start of September, up 13% year-on-year and just below May’s all-time high of 210.4m cgt. China captured 74% of new cgt contracted over the preceding 12 months, lifting its share of the global orderbook to 64%, against South Korea’s 19% and Japan’s 6%. Containerships account for 30% of tonnage on order and 68% of the past year’s growth. BIMCO calculates that Chinese yards hold orders equivalent to 4.2 years of recent peak annual production, compared with 1.9 years in South Korea and 1.7 in Japan. Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44m cgt in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m cgt delivered in 2025 “Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44m cgt in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m cgt delivered in 2025,” said BIMCO chief shipping analyst Niels Rasmussen, warning that the necessary capacity expansion risks leaving yards underutilised when contracting eventually slows. The squeeze is already bringing new shipbuilders into the tanker market. Veson Nautical reports that 51 vessels have been ordered at newly entering yards this year, up 34% from 2025. Eleven of the 16 yards identified are Chinese. The standout is Hengli Shipbuilding, which delivered its first vessel in 2024 and now holds an extraordinary 495-ship orderbook valued at $46bn. “Owners’ willingness to place orders at yards without an established tanker track record likely reflects capacity constraints at established tanker-building yards,” observed Veson analyst Rebecca Galanopoulos. Yet, despite the rush, tanker newbuilding prices remain surprisingly affordable relative to historical peaks. Broker Affinity noted in a recent research note that VLCC newbuilding prices are still 20% to 25% below their 2008 highs in nominal terms, despite today’s unprecedented tanker earnings. Adjusted for inflation, a $160m VLCC in 2008 would cost roughly $250m today, nearly double current prices. Affinity argued that Hengli’s enormous capacity injection has restrained prices, although disappearing early delivery slots and shortages of engines and pumps could soon trigger another upward move. articles.body: Greater China Shipyards China adds new state-owned shipbuilding player in Guangzhou Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 556 1 minute read Guangzhou SASAC Guangzhou SASAC Guangzhou has formally launched a new state-owned maritime industrial group as the southern Chinese shipbuilding hub looks to expand its manufacturing capacity and bring more of the industry’s supply chain under local ownership. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group, established with registered capital of RMB2bn ($300m), has begun operations following an unveiling ceremony this week. The company is wholly owned by Guangzhou Industrial Investment Holding Group, with the municipal government as its ultimate shareholder. It was incorporated in July but has now formally launched its operations and signed a series of cooperation agreements. The new group has joined forces with China State Shipbuilding Corporation-controlled Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) and Huangpu Wenchong, as well as COSCO Shipping Specialized Carriers, marine technology company SEAHI Robotics and the Guangzhou branch of China Classification Society. The move is intended to strengthen Guangzhou’s position in shipbuilding by combining local manufacturing assets with investment and maritime services. The group will draw on businesses involved in marine propulsion, heavy engineering and shipboard equipment, including Guangzhou Diesel Engine Factory, while expanding into vessel retrofits, equipment maintenance, industrial park development, leasing and inspection services. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group has set a target of reaching about $3.9bn in business scale by 2030, according to local government-backed reporting. The launch comes alongside a major expansion of the city’s shipbuilding infrastructure. Guangzhou is developing a new marine equipment manufacturing and shipbuilding base at Longxue North in Nansha, involving investment of approximately $1.09bn. The project was launched in September and is being developed separately from the new group’s establishment. GSI is lined up to operate the facility, which is expected to be completed in 2029. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group is also lined up to participate in the development, although its financial commitment has not been disclosed. The latest move follows a series of investments by Guangzhou’s established shipbuilders to deal with bulging orderbooks. GSI recently signed an agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group to outsource hull block production, adding manufacturing capacity outside the traditional shipbuilding supply chain. The yard has also been expanding its physical footprint, with new facilities planned at Xiaohudao and Longxue North as construction slots stretch towards 2030. articles.title: A new world order emerges in LNG shipping
articles.summary: The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British...
articles.body: Gas A new world order emerges in LNG shipping Sam Chambers October 22, 2026 0 645 3 minutes read Teo Malnar Teo Malnar The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British thermal units, LNG carrier spot earnings remain remarkably weak, with the Baltic Exchange assessing the US Gulf-Europe route at just $21,200 a day last week. Nearly eight months into the Hormuz crisis, oil exporters have found ways around the chokepoint. Kpler estimates that non-Iranian Middle Eastern oil flows, including alternative routes, recovered to prewar levels last week. LNG remains a different proposition, with Qatar unable to replicate the pipelines and offshore transfers that have restored much of the region’s crude trade. Vortexa recorded just five confirmed LNG carrier transits of Hormuz last week, against a four-week average of 12. Only two were laden outbound voyages. Ras Laffan loaded five cargoes totalling 400,000 tonnes. Kpler identified 13 Qatari LNG loadings during October 1-13, but only four ships were broadcasting active AIS signals. The remaining nine were verified through satellite imagery, tug tracking and other intelligence. The Al Kharsaah, carrying Qatari LNG towards Poland via the Red Sea, came under fire from a small boat in the Gulf of Aden on October 17. Its armed security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. The voyage could deliver Europe’s first Qatari cargo since April. The disruption is now being measured in cancelled contracts as well as missing ships. Italy’s Edison has received force majeure notices covering 35 Qatari LNG cargoes, equivalent to 4.6bn cu m of gas, with deliveries suspended until early December. Damage inflicted on two liquefaction trains at Ras Laffan in March has also removed 12.8m tonnes of annual production capacity, with repairs potentially taking years. The US is meanwhile cementing its position as the indispensable swing supplier. American terminals dispatched 2.5m tonnes across 36 cargoes last week, according to Vortexa, while official US figures show exports surged 23% in the first half of 2026. There is an irony in the American resurgence. QatarEnergy owns 70% of Golden Pass in Texas, where an expanding export operation is helping diversify its supply portfolio beyond the troubled Gulf. Europe is capturing an increasing share of Atlantic supply. S&P Global data shows Europe and Turkey received 76 of the 143 US LNG cargoes delivered in September. Egypt has also become a major destination, taking 14 American cargoes during the month as declining domestic production increases its dependence on imported gas. The reshuffle is particularly visible in India. Oman, whose LNG terminals sit outside Hormuz, displaced the US as India’s largest supplier in September. Kpler recorded 590,000 tonnes arriving from Oman, compared with 350,000 tonnes from Nigeria and 340,000 tonnes from the US. Qatar, once India’s dominant supplier, managed just 100,000 tonnes. Not all Asian buyers are responding alike. Indian LNG imports were 7% higher year-on-year in September despite elevated prices. China, Japan and South Korea have proved more reluctant to chase expensive spot cargoes. Japan’s major utilities held 2.64m tonnes of LNG in inventory earlier this month, their highest stockpile since December 2023. South Korea is increasingly relying on coal generation, with Kpler projecting available coal plant utilisation of 63.5% in November and December. IFCHOR Galbraiths calculates that South Korean coal imports rose 14% year-on-year during January-September, while Japan’s increased 8%. China’s September LNG imports fell to 5.2m tonnes, according to Kpler, as weaker industrial demand and growing pipeline supplies reduced its need for seaborne gas. Europe has less flexibility. Gas storage was just 74.6% full this week, nearly 15 percentage points below its five-year seasonal average, with Germany at around 61%. A cold winter would intensify competition for Atlantic cargoes, particularly as the EU prepares to end remaining Russian LNG imports from January 1. Stronger European demand for US gas has shortened average Atlantic voyages, releasing vessels back into the market more quickly and depressing tonne-mile demand. Baltic Exchange assessments last week put the US Gulf-Japan route at $49,000 a day, more than twice the equivalent European route. Fleet expansion adds another complication. Flex LNG estimates the global orderbook at approximately 285 vessels, equivalent to 37% of the existing fleet, with around 95 deliveries expected next year. Beyond the immediate crisis, another geographical shift is gathering momentum. LNG Canada’s September investment decision to double capacity to 28m tonnes annually reinforces the emergence of a Pacific export corridor offering Asian customers shorter voyages than traditional Atlantic suppliers. Meanwhile, Europe’s Russian LNG ban could force Arctic cargoes towards more distant Asian destinations, creating fresh shipping demand but also logistical and sanctions-related complications. The emerging picture for LNG shipping is one of greater geographical diversification, increasingly unpredictable cargo movements and an uncomfortable mismatch between the price of gas and the value of carrying it. articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 22, 2026 · 9 hours ago $6 billion deepwater oil project crosses 50% mark as Angolan partners track subsea gear’s buildout progress TotalEnergies, Petronas, Sonangol, and ANPG have inspected the manufacturing progress of subsea equipment at OneSubsea’s facility. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Visit to OneSubsea's facilities in Malaysia Source: ANPG A multibillion-dollar oil project off the coast of Angola has passed the halfway development mark, as France’s TotalEnergies, Malaysia’s Petroliam Nasional Berhad (Petronas), Luanda-headquartered Sonangol EP, and the country’s National Agency of Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG) headed overseas to check on the construction of critical subsea hardware for the African project. A delegation from ANPG, led by Administrator Ana Miala , together with representatives from TotalEnergies, Petronas, and Sonangol visited the OneSubsea facilities in Johor, Republic of Malaysia, at the end of last month to monitor the manufacturing of equipment that integrates the subsea production system (SPS) of the Kaminho project. The delegation included Gaspar Fernandes , Member of the Operations Committee for Block 20 of ANPG; Mutombo Dondo , Deputy Director of TotalEnergies EP Angola; Rui Rodrigues and Steven Croguennec , Directors of Block 20 at TotalEnergies EP Angola and of the project, respectively; and representatives of the Block 20/11 partners from Petronas and Sonangol. Visit to OneSubsea's facilities was made to check on the progress of the subsea production system for Kaminho; Courtesy of ANPG During the visit, the delegation confirmed the planned schedule for the arrival in Angola, starting in 2027, of the equipment currently in production at OneSubsea's facilities in Malaysia. Before its offshore installation, this equipment will be tested by Angolan OneSubsea teams at the company's testing facilities in Sonils, Luanda. Among the components being manufactured are 13 subsea Christmas trees, with a focus on safety, quality, and delivery of said equipment within the planned deadlines. The execution of the Kaminho project has already exceeded 50%. The Kaminho project's subsea production system will be installed at a depth greater than 1,500 meters and will connect the wells of the Cameia reservoir to the system of pipelines that carry hydrocarbons to the FPSO Kaminho to allow them to be treated and separated into water, gas, and crude oil. Related Articles Fossil Energy All-electric FPSO for TotalEnergies’ Angolan project starts taking shape in China 3 min read Following national and international legislation, after treatment the water will be discharged back into the sea, the gas will be fully reinjected into the reservoir with no routine flaring, and the crude oil will be stored in the FPSO hull and then exported to an oil tanker. Located in Block 20/11, about 100 kilometers off the Angolan coast, Kaminho is scheduled to come online in 2028. With an investment of approximately $6 billion, this is the first major deepwater oil project in the Kwanza Basin, which is expected to open doors to new investment in the Angolan frontier . Among the companies blacklisted is Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading, the Panama- and Greece-based manager of seven Panama-flagged bulk carriers and general cargo ships. Treasury also linked the company to networks associated with Iranian shipping figure Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line was designated for supporting Amigoz and acting as shipping agent for a company accused of arranging Iranian petrochemical purchases. Its two UAE-flagged support vessels, Whales Diamond and Whales Pearl, were also blacklisted. The action forms part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August, which is intended to cut Iran off from international financial and shipping services. US authorities are simultaneously investigating a Greek bank’s possible links with Iran, underlining the campaign’s extension from ships and owners to lawyers, agents and financiers. It expects mid-to-high single-digit organic revenue growth, improved adjusted operating margins at constant exchange rates and strong cash flow generation. The company has set a target of generating €1 billion in revenue from AI-driven markets and services by 2030. It has also upgraded its total revenue growth target at constant currency to a double-digit compound annual growth rate for 2027–2028. “The third quarter of 2026 marks another quarter of solid execution, with organic revenue growth of 6.2% in a volatile geopolitical and macroeconomic environment,” said Hinda Gharbi, Chief Executive Officer of Bureau Veritas. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal reported growth in vessel traffic, tonnage and revenue in fiscal year 2026, as stronger demand from energy carriers and containerships helped lift volumes despite ongoing concerns over water availability. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the fiscal year ended September 30, up 4.1% from 13,404 the previous year, according to results released Wednesday by the Panama Canal Authority. Total tonnage climbed 6.5% to 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, compared with 489.2 million tons in fiscal 2025. Larger vessels continued to drive much of the growth. Ships using the canal’s Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with volumes through those locks increasing 8.2% year over year. The canal attributed the gains to stronger demand from energy shipping segments, solid containership performance and shifting international trade patterns. Financial results were even stronger, with total revenue reaching approximately $6.6 billion, up 16.6% from the previous year. The figures remain unaudited. The results come as the canal continues to balance growing shipping demand with water conservation measures designed to protect operations during the developing El Niño weather pattern. Despite the challenges, the canal maintained a maximum authorized draft of 50 feet throughout the fiscal year’s dry season, providing relatively stable operating conditions for shipping customers. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta said during a conference call hosted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. The canal also announced Wednesday that it was immediately reinstating its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service allows vessels without existing reservations to secure a transit slot when one becomes available, although the canal retains discretion over whether to offer the additional capacity. The decision follows improvements in watershed conditions, with recent rainfall approaching average levels and water-saving measures helping conserve supplies. It marks another adjustment to operations following restrictions imposed earlier this year in response to below-normal rainfall. The canal recently increased daily booking capacity to 33 slots , including 10 Neopanamax slots, effective October 15. However, water availability remains a concern. The canal has warned that a continuing water deficit could require further operational adjustments, particularly if El Niño conditions intensify. During Wednesday’s call, canal executives also discussed longer-term infrastructure investments, including the proposed Río Indio Lake Project, a central component of the canal’s strategy to secure freshwater supplies for future operations. The project is part of the canal’s broader Vision 2025–2035 development plan, aimed at strengthening the waterway’s resilience and maintaining its competitiveness as global shipping patterns evolve. For now, the latest results show that the Panama Canal continues to attract growing volumes of shipping traffic, even as water management remains one of its biggest operational challenges.
